title: The more options you give, the less people buy
_format: 1080x1350 = 4:5. NICHT 3:4 — die Instagram-API akzeptiert beim automatischen Veroeffentlichen nur 4:5 bis 1.91:1. Bildprompts bleiben 3:4, ihre schwarze Fusszone faengt die Differenz ab.
_syntax: [Klammern] = Akzentfarbe mit Textur (nur in headline). **Sterne** = fett in bullets/body. Zeilenumbruch = eigener Array-Eintrag. `alt` pro Slide ist Pflicht — Buffer verlangt altText beim Upload.

caption.kern: A fancy grocery store set up a tasting table. One day: 24 jam flavors. The next: just 6. The big table drew a crowd — and almost nobody bought anything. 🍯
caption.detail: Psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper ran the tasting booths on separate days in 2000. About 60% of shoppers stopped at the 24-flavor table versus 40% at the 6-flavor one. But only 3% of the big-table tasters bought a jar — versus 40% at the small table. Ten times the conversion, with a quarter of the flavors.
caption.kontext: This is why bigger menus, longer feeds, and endless product pages don't feel like abundance after a while — they feel like a low hum of dread. Every extra option is one more way to have chosen wrong.
caption.frage: When did more choices last make a decision harder, not easier?
caption.sources: Sources: Iyengar, S.S. & Lepper, M.R. — When Choice is Demotivating: Can One Desire Too Much of a Good Thing? • Journal of Personality and Social Psychology 79(6): 995-1006, 2000

headline: THE MORE OPTIONS YOU GIVE,
THE [LESS PEOPLE BUY]
slides.sub: A GROCERY STORE PROVED IT BY ACCIDENT. 2000.
slides.alt: A single jam jar glowing warmly in dark void, TBD final concept. Headline: The more options you give, the less people buy.

headline: [24] FLAVORS DREW
[MORE] LOOKS
slides.body: Iyengar and Lepper put 24 jams on a tasting table in an upscale grocery store. [60%] of passing shoppers stopped, against [40%] at a table with only six. By every measure of attention, the big display won.
slides.alt: A wide tasting table crowded with two dozen jam jars, TBD final concept. Headline: 24 flavors drew more looks.

headline: BUT [FEWER]
OF THEM BOUGHT
slides.body: Only [3%] of the 24-flavor tasters actually bought a jar. At the six-flavor table it was [40%] — more than [ten times as many], from a quarter of the options.
slides.alt: A single hand confidently picking one jar from a small row, TBD final concept. Headline: But fewer of them bought.

headline: MORE OPTIONS ISN'T
THE SAME AS
[MORE FREEDOM]
slides.body: More choice looks like more freedom. In practice it is more work — comparing, second-guessing, imagining the jar you didn't pick. Past a certain point options don't help you decide. [They give you permission not to].
slides.alt: An empty tasting table at closing, unsold jars, TBD final concept. Headline: More options isn't the same as more freedom.

headline: PICKING FROM [6] FELT LIKE
A DECISION. PICKING FROM [24]
FELT LIKE [WORK].
slides.tag: WE SHARE DAILY FINDINGS FROM THE WORLD OF PSYCHOLOGY.
slides.alt: A wooden kitchen table in warm morning light with a glass of water, an open notebook and pen, and folded reading glasses. Headline: Picking from six felt like a decision, picking from 24 felt like work.
